PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 77 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 09/14/25 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up visit for COPD management, evaluation of lower extremity edema, and assessment of persistent fatigue.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax presents for a follow-up visit regarding his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), ongoing bilateral lower extremity edema, and persistent fatigue. Since his last appointment, he reports a slight worsening of his respiratory symptoms, particularly noting an increase in wheezing episodes, especially during the night. He has been compliant with his albuterol inhaler, using it twice daily, and continues with his fluticasone/salmeterol regimen; however, he expresses concern over the recent increase in nocturnal symptoms.
Mr. Fairfax reports that his lower extremity edema has shown minimal improvement despite an increased furosemide dosage to 60 mg daily. The edema remains at 1+ pitting and is particularly bothersome by the end of the day. He denies any associated pain, erythema, or warmth but is worried about the persistent swelling and its impact on his mobility.
Regarding his fatigue, Mr. Fairfax continues to experience generalized tiredness. He reports that the fatigue is exacerbated by increased physical activity and is not alleviated by rest. He notes no recent changes in weight, appetite, or sleep patterns, but he has been feeling less motivated to engage in his usual light activities.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + fatigue, no fevers or chills. Pulmonary - + increased wheezing, - cough, - sputum production, - dyspnea on exertion, no hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain or palpitations, + orthopnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - + joint pain in knees and hands, no swelling. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) 2. Hypertension 3. Osteoarthritis 4. Persistent fatigue
PAST SURGICAL HISTORY
1. Right knee arthroscopy in 2018.
FAMILY HISTORY
Father - history of lung cancer. Mother - history of hypertension.
SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives alone in , . Former carpenter, now retired. Quit smoking 15 years ago. Occasional alcohol use. No illicit drug use.
ALLERGIES
No known drug allergies.
MEDICATIONS ON FOLLOW-UP
1. Albuterol inhaler as needed, increased use to twice daily 2. Lisinopril 20 mg daily 3. Fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 MDI, 1 puff twice daily 4. Acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for pain 5. Furosemide 60 mg daily
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: T 98.7F, HR 80, BP 128/78, RR 20, O2 sat 92% on room air
General: Elderly male in no acute distress but appears fatigued. HEENT: No nasal congestion, oropharynx clear. Pulmonary: Diminished breath sounds bilaterally, moderate wheezing noted on expiration, no crackles. Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs. Extremities: 1+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities, no erythema or warmth.
LABORATORY DATA
1. CBC: WBC 8.8, Hgb 12.9, Hct 38.0, Plt 220 2. BMP: Na 135, K 4.0, Cl 97, CO2 25, BUN 18, Cr 1.2, Glucose 90 3. BNP: 420 (slightly increased). 4. Thyroid function tests: TSH 3.6 (within normal limits).
ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. COPD management: Due to the recent increase in wheezing and nocturnal symptoms, consider adding a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) or increasing the fluticasone/salmeterol dosage. Reassess inhaler technique and adherence. Follow-up in 1 month. 2. Hypertension: Continue lisinopril. Blood pressure remains well-controlled. Follow-up in 1 month. 3. Lower extremity edema: As the edema persists despite increased furosemide, consider referral to a nephrologist for further evaluation of potential underlying causes. Reinforce dietary sodium restrictions and encourage Mr. Fairfax to elevate his legs when possible. 4. Fatigue: Given the stable thyroid function tests and no signs of anemia, consider a referral to physical therapy to address deconditioning and improve activity tolerance. Schedule a follow-up CBC and metabolic panel in one month to monitor for any changes.
Patient education reinforced regarding the importance of recognizing exacerbation signs, adherence to medication, and lifestyle modifications to manage COPD and edema effectively.
